title: Looking for the more "expressionistic" films noirs out there

commenti.body: [removed]

Aim for the more auteur directors of the noir movement.

Orson Welles' Touch of Evil

Jules Dassin's Night and the City

Billy Wilder's Sunset Boulevard

And if you want to read a great book that delves deep into the world, check out James Narremore's More Than Night

'Leave Her to Heaven' is a gorgeous Technicolor noir, with beautiful cinematography and a moody, gothic tone that is unforgettable.

I think Nicholas Ray's noir outings could also scratch your itch, especially 'In A Lonely Place'.

I would be remiss not to include my favorite adaptation of 'The Killers' (1946), which has some incredible expressionistic passages.

A great film noir I saw recently and which I had never heard of before is from Argentina called The Bitter Stems, it's from 1956 and you can read about it in the link below. It wasn't difficult to find with English subtitles via the usual high seas voyages...it's something a bit different, highly recommended. Another one that's got some noir elements but isn't really noir as such is an odd little Britih film from 1953 called The Yellow Balloon which has some great location shooting in a bombed out London. It was directed by J Lee Thompson who went on to do all sorts...it's definitley expressionistic lots of dramatic scenes lighting shadows and a great climax...

Kiss Me Deadly is surely a winner - well, they all are, but KMD in particular seems to tick OP’s boxes. I might throw in Key Largo for the “otherworldly mood” angle - the setting is obviously a part of that, but I think Edward G. Robinson is the main factor. According to David Thomson’s review Huston described Robinson as looking like “a crustacean out of its shell”, which captures an ugly character beautifully (as a noir should).

Please tell me that you're aware of Alphaville? judging by what you're asking for it's perfect for you. It's a black and white dystopian sci-fi crime thriller and my god does it deliver in every possible facet of filmmaking.  

I would also highly recommended the films of Val Lewton, producer auteur. He makes movies that always tease the supernatural but never are. Cat People is his most famous film and its great but my favorite of his is "Ghost Ship" or "The Body Snatcher"

 Here are a few more though that may or may not be up your alley

Gun Crazy

Tokyo Drifter (or any of the Seijun Suzuki's Yakuza films)

The Cremator

and one last curve ball (pun intended) Rollerball from 1975 is another arguably dystopian sci-fi film that has a lot of film-noir elements imo.

I love Welles’ The Lady from Shanghai and it definitely has a few fairly expressionistic sequences, most notably the funhouse scene with infinity mirrors at the end. I love a lot of other noirs too but if the classics listed above like Sunset Blvd and Touch of Evil aren’t quite up your alley, you’re probably not going to find a ton in the genre that excites you.

Tokyo Drifter is a great recommendation, I love how that movie feels like it’s remixing noir iconography with this poppy, French New Wave sensibility and also of course lots of very Japanese elements.

This feels like a bit of an obvious one but I don’t think anyones recommended it yet - what about Boorman’s *Point Blank*? It’s a classic noir narrative but the imagery and sound design feels almost experimental at points, lots of non-linear editing and weird lighting/framing.

Your taste actually sounds not too dissimilar to mine here, love nouvelle vague, german expression and genre cinema. Some noirs can be a bit formal sometimes, I'm thinking a bit of Wilder as I write this even though I think his films are actually very good. I too like the more unhinged ones better. 

A no-brainer but also cheating would be **Elevator to the Gallows** (1958) which a lot of people wouldn't consider real noir because it's a french film but you got a Miles Davis soundtrack, Jeanne Moureau and an incredible sense of urgency in one of Malle's finest works which I can't recommend enough.

Apart from that I think Samuel Fuller sounds excactly like what you're searching for. There's a reason he got to feature in Godard's Pierrot le Fou, he's like an American Bresson but turned entirely on its head, very rough around the edges, usually on a shoestring budget but with a lot of force and compassion for real material struggles and not a lot of respect for formalities or rules. My favourite is **Naked Kiss** (1964) which again arguably is not a noir because it's made after 1958 but these classification rules suck anyway. The most zany, bold and otherworldy one is probably **Shock Corridor** (1963) set in an insane asylum. A slightly more classical noir but told to perfection with force and brevity would be **Underworld USA** (1961) which is arguably much better than it has any right to be. Also ofc **Pickup on South Street** (1953) is a must, though it plays a bit more by the numbers than the later ones but still has Fuller plastered allover it and can't help liking it a lot.

I feel similarly about Tourneur, Ray and Huston but don't know if their greatest accomplishments are in noir territory quite as much as Fuller's. **I Walked with a Zombie** (1943) is one of the greatest films of all times and definitely has a lot of noir attributes, at least asteathically, though it's more of a horror film. **The Seventh Victim** (1947) btw also. which is an astoundingly sinister film about simply vanishing, particularly when you crosswatch it with Rivette's **Duelle** (1976) which is his take on noir influenced by the former. Though it ocassionally feels kind of amateurish compared to Tourneur's work. Ray's **In a Lonely Place** (1950) and **They Live by Night** (1948) are obvious mentions but I feel they pale slightly against Johnny Guitar and Bigger than Life which push both the melodrama and the socioeconomic forces in the tale much more forcefully, still great work.

as for some others:

* Cheating again but everything Cluzot. Le Corbeau (1943) and Quai des Orfèvres (1947) are overlooked. Les diaboliques (1955) is a no-brainer. Try the **Inferno documentary** (2009) too. That would have been excactly the film you're searching for but unfortunately Cluzot got a breakdown while making it. [This](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0HtumDL5Oy8) should give you an idea.

* Mildread Piearce (1945) - Because Curtiz' is a lunatic. Crazy kind of film.

* If you have any love for heist movies The Killing (1956) and Rififi (1955). 

* The Lady From Shanghai (1947) - one of the Welles films that feels the most finished, fantastically modern, amazing atmosphere. Rivette also borrows a scene almost directly from that one in Duelle.

* The Wrong Man (1956), Strangers on a Train (1951) and Shadow of a Doubt (1943) by Hitchcock - a bit less zany but I'd be damned if this is not compelling.

* Kiss me Deadly (1955), The Prowler (1952), Gilda (1945), Shoot the Piano Player (1960), also try some Lang, Woman by the Window (1944) has always been my favourite but admittedly he's much better in Germany.

* Also arguably this is just German expressionism in the USA by German emigrants and not noir but Dreams that Money can buy (1947) definitely ticks all the boxes you're writing about but it might be even more crazy than what you're looking for.
Fantastic post, thank you! I'll look into all of this.
